 She Loses $180,000 to an Investment Scam at 74, as Older Adults Report $3 Billion in Fraud Losses. The Same Scammers Often Come Back for Her Social Security Deposit, and One Online Request Can Lock Changes to Her $2,170 Monthly Check
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published November 14, 2026, 7:38pm ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Older adults reported about $3 billion in fraud losses in 2025, and scammers often return to target victims' Social Security deposits.
 One request to block electronic access to Social Security records stops online deposit changes, protecting a lifetime, inflation-adjusted check worth roughly $651,000 in portfolio terms.
 Extra retirement withdrawals to cover losses can make up to 85% of benefits taxable and raise Medicare premiums two years later.

 Say, at 74, she wired $180,000 into what looked like a professional trading platform, with a dashboard showing her balance climbing weekly. When she tried to withdraw, the site asked for a release fee and then went silent. The money is gone. She still has a $2,170 Social Security deposit that lands every month, and that check is what scammers will try to reach next.
 She has plenty of company. In October 2026, the Federal Trade Commission reported adults 60 and older reported about $3 billion in fraud losses for 2025, including more than $1 billion from investment scams.
 Investment scam losses jumped 42% in a single year. In one widely reported case, a San Jose widow lost almost her entire life savings. A scammer posing as an online romantic interest had manipulated her.
 Her Monthly Check Now Outweighs Everything She Lost
 A little rough math puts the loss in perspective, as a common rule of thumb lets a retiree draw about 4% of savings a year. On the stolen savings, that comes to roughly $600 a month. Her Social Security pays more than three times that, or $26,040 a year.
 To produce that same income from a portfolio at a 4% draw, she would need about $651,000. The scam took a big portion of her savings, but her largest retirement asset is intact. It pays for as long as she lives and rises with inflation. The 2027 inflation adjustment is 3.6%.
 That changes the priority. Getting the stolen money back is unlikely. Making sure nobody redirects the check is entirely within her control.
 Scammers Come Back for the Deposit, and One Request Shuts the Door
 Fraud victims often get targeted a second time. Refund and recovery scammers buy lists of people who’ve already been scammed, then call and promise to recover the money for an upfront fee. Some also ask for her Social Security number and bank details to process the refund. With those, a criminal can try to get into her online Social Security account and send her deposit to a new bank.
 Social Security lets beneficiaries block electronic access to their records, which stops online changes to direct deposit. Once the block is in place, it locks you out of your own online account too. After that, any change to her payment has to go through Social Security directly, where her identity is verified first. She can set it up with a single request.
 Preventing the theft matters more than trying to recover the money later. In complaints reviewed by federal regulators, companies often denied liability for losses stemming from scams or said they could not reverse fraudulent transfers. A redirects deposit may never come back.
 How the Withdrawal Raises Her Taxes and Medicare Bill
 If the money came from a pretax retirement account, the IRS counts the withdrawal as income, even though a criminal ended up with it. That extra income can make up to 85% of the social security benefits [ 1 ] she receives taxable under 26 U.S.C. § 86(a)(2), on top of the tax on the withdrawal itself. A New Jersey widow who lost $2 million to scammers ended up owing $117K in taxes , thought the state later waived the balance.
 Medicare costs go up too, two years later. Part B premiums are based on income from two years earlier. Under the 2026 tiers, a single filer with income between $171,000 and $205,000 [ 2 ] pays $528 a month instead of the standard $203.
 That surcharge works out to about $3,895 a year, and it comes straight out of her Social Security deposit. Social Security does take appeals for investment property lost to fraud, but it asks for proof of conviction, which many scam victims never get. A tax preparer can also check whether the loss qualifies as a deductible theft loss.
 Two Moves That Protect Her Next Payment
 First, put the electronic access block in place before anyone calls offering help, because any recovery offer that asks for a fee, gift cards, or account details is part of the scam. Government agencies do not charge to take a fraud report.
 Second, wait before pulling more money from retirement accounts to make up the loss. Each extra withdrawal this year can raise the tax on her benefits and her Medicare premiums two years from now. Both costs come out of the one income source the scammers could not take.
 Her actual tax bill, premium tier, and appeal options depend on which account the money came from and what other income she has. A short review with a tax professional before she files can catch costs that are easy to miss.
